sections.overview: The Arctic fox is a small northern canid whose circumpolar range follows treeless tundra from North America and Greenland across Eurasia to Iceland and other Arctic islands. Compact proportions, dense fur and furry feet help it remain active through severe winters.
sections.identification: Short ears, a short muzzle, low-set legs and a very full tail give it a rounded outline. Most foxes moult between a brownish summer coat and thick white winter fur; the blue morph stays charcoal or brown-grey year-round, lightening somewhat in winter. Fur also covers the foot soles. The Norwegian Polar Institute reports a body length of about 60 cm plus a tail near 30 cm, and a body mass of 2.5–5 kg. The account gives no sex-specific adult range or body width.
sections.habitat: It occupies Arctic and alpine tundra, from inland valleys to coasts, barren islands and, seasonally, sea ice. Dens are excavated in raised, well-drained ground and may be reused for generations. In Svalbard, foxes range from mountain ridges to shorelines and drifting ice.
sections.diet: Food changes with place and season. Inland lemming foxes depend heavily on cyclic lemmings and voles; coastal foxes also take seabirds, eggs, fish, marine carrion and terrestrial prey. Berries and cached food add variety. Coastal supplies peak in summer and become scarcer in winter.
sections.behavior: Breeding pairs defend territories around dens, but Arctic foxes can roam widely when food is scarce and travel over sea ice. They scavenge as well as hunt, and may hide surplus food among rocks or in dens. Outside the breeding season, individuals often forage alone.
sections.reproduction: Mating generally occurs in late winter or early spring; after about 52–54 days, pups are born in a den in May or June. They first emerge at three to four weeks and are weaned around four to six weeks. Litter size responds strongly to food: inland lemming populations fluctuate more than coastal ones.
sections.ecology: As both predator and scavenger, the fox links tundra and marine food webs. Inland populations follow rodent cycles, while coastal populations can use seabird colonies and reindeer carcasses; these alternative foods can stabilize numbers. Predation may affect ground-nesting birds, with effects depending on local prey and conditions.
sections.conservation: The IUCN global assessment, last assessed in 2023 and published in 2025, lists the species as Least Concern. This broad category masks sharp regional differences: the 2021 Norwegian Red List classified mainland Norway’s population as Critically Endangered, while Svalbard’s was Least Concern. Fennoscandian populations receive intensive conservation measures.
